title: Baba Dayal
hook: a reformer in Rawalpindi taught worship of the formless God and simple Sikh ceremonies; his followers were called Nirankaris
tomorrow: Baba Ram Singh and the Namdharis

segments.voice: Yesterday, ratan, a jewel: the long stretch of loss and exile closed with something found again. Today a new part of the story opens: reform and renewal.

A shopkeeper in Rawalpindi, in the north of the Punjab, keeps saying the same thing to anyone who stops by. God has no shape. God is not in the stone figure on the shelf, or in the ritual the priest charges for. God is Nirankar, without form, just as the Gurus sang. His name is Baba Dayal. He isn't raising an army or building a palace. He's asking people to strip their worship back to what the Gurus taught. The people who listened came to be called Nirankaris.
screen: `A SHOPKEEPER IN RAWALPINDI.` → `GOD HAS NO SHAPE.` → `STRIP WORSHIP BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Nirankar is a name for God in the Guru Granth Sahib: the formless One. In the Japji, Guru Nanak closes several verses by calling God the formless one who lives forever. Nirankari simply means a person devoted to that formless One. Second, what Baba Dayal saw. Histories of the period describe Sikh homes and shrines that kept images, costly rites, and Brahmin priests hired for births, weddings and deaths. Many Sikhs then saw no conflict in that. To Baba Dayal, it was drifting away from the Gurus. Third, what he taught: remember the formless God and repeat the Name. Drop the images. Keep the ceremonies simple. His followers became known for weddings held before the Guru Granth Sahib, the couple walking around the scripture as hymns are sung, the rite Sikhs call Anand Karaj. Some historians count Baba Dayal among the early reformers of the Sikh revival, and the Nirankaris kept his teaching alive in their own circle. Fourth, a name to keep straight. A much later group in Punjab also uses the word Nirankari in its name. It's a separate movement, and the two shouldn't be mixed up; here, Nirankari means Baba Dayal and those who followed him. Reform doesn't always start with a speech. Sometimes it starts with one person taking things away, the extra objects, the extra fees, the extra noise, until what's left is what was meant to be there all along.
screen: `NIRANKAR — THE FORMLESS ONE.` · `CUSTOMS HE SAW AS DRIFT.` · `THE NAME, AND SIMPLE CEREMONIES.` · `NOT THE LATER GROUP OF THAT NAME.` · then, large: `BACK TO THE FORMLESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one daily habit that has gathered extra steps over time, the morning scroll, the way you eat lunch, the way you pray or don't, and ask what it was for in the first place. Picture it with just one extra step gone, and breathe slowly while you look at the simpler version. If you pray, repeat Waheguru on each breath out, with nothing added.
Nirankari. One devoted to Nirankar, the formless God, and the name given to the followers of Baba Dayal of Rawalpindi. Today's word.
Your line: back to the formless. No shape, no fee, only the Name. Day nine hundred fifty-seven, done.
